title: Splitting a network, and the arithmetic behind it
objective: By the end of this lesson you can split a range into subnets in your head, say which subnet any address belongs to, and allocate unequal blocks without wasting addresses.

blocks.text: Subnetting has a reputation for being difficult, and it is not. It is one operation — moving the boundary between the network part and the host part — repeated. Everything else is arithmetic you can do without a calculator once you see the pattern.
Moving the boundary by one bit halves the block
Each bit you take from the host part doubles the number of subnets and halves the size of each. That single sentence generates the whole table you would otherwise memorise.

rows: 0, 4, 8, 12, ... — used for links between two routers

blocks.title: The one number worth carrying in your head
blocks.text: The block size. A /26 has a block size of 64, so its networks start at 0, 64, 128 and 192 — nothing else is possible. Knowing the block size lets you answer every other question by counting, without converting anything to binary.

blocks.caption: 192.0.2.0/24 divided into /26 blocks — computed, not recalled
lines: /* Each block is 64 wide. The first address in each is the network,
the last is the broadcast, and the 62 in between go to machines. */

blocks.text: Which subnet does an address belong to?
Divide the last octet by the block size, discard the remainder, and multiply back. That is the whole method — no binary required.

blocks.caption: Four addresses, block size 64
lines: /* All four verified against a subnet calculator. */

blocks.title: The case that catches people: a prefix that is not a multiple of 8
blocks.text: 172.16.5.0/20 does not describe a network starting at 172.16.5.0. With a /20 the block size in the third octet is 16, so the networks start at 172.16.0.0, 172.16.16.0, 172.16.32.0 and so on — and 172.16.5.0 falls inside the first one. Verified: its network is 172.16.0.0 and its broadcast is 172.16.15.255, covering 4096 addresses. Two more of the same kind: 10.1.200.0/22 gives network 10.1.200.0 and broadcast 10.1.203.255; 192.168.7.130/25 gives network 192.168.7.128 and broadcast 192.168.7.255.
Unequal blocks: allocating what each group needs

Splitting a range into equal pieces wastes addresses when the groups are different sizes. Allocating variable-sized blocks — largest first, each aligned to its own size — fits them all in without waste.

blocks.caption: Carving 198.51.100.0/24 for four groups
lines: link to router needs   2 -> 198.51.100.224/30   gives   2 usable
/* Largest first, and each block starts at a multiple of its own size.
Allocate smallest first and the alignment breaks. */

blocks.text: That /30 at the end is worth noticing: four addresses, of which two are usable, which is exactly what a link between two routers needs. It is the smallest useful subnet, and you will see a lot of them in real networks.

blocks.caption: How many smaller blocks fit inside a larger one
lines: /* The rule: 2 raised to the difference in prefix length.
Splitting a /24 into /26 blocks gives 2^(26-24) = 4, which matches above. */

blocks.title: Do it by hand, then check yourself
steps: Split 10.0.0.0/24 into eight equal subnets — what prefix, and what are the eight network addresses?
For 10.0.0.0/27, work out the block size, then say which subnet 10.0.0.100 is in
Work out the network and broadcast of 172.20.30.40/21 without a calculator
Check all three with: ipcalc <address>/<prefix>   or python3 -c "import ipaddress; print(ipaddress.ip_interface('...').network)"
Design an allocation from 192.168.10.0/24 for: 60 desktops, 25 phones, 10 servers, and two router links
Verify no two of your blocks overlap and each is aligned to its own size
Run: ip route     and read each line as a network address plus a prefix
For one route in that output, say which addresses it covers
blocks.expected: Eight /27 networks at 0, 32, 64, 96, 128, 160, 192 and 224; an allocation with no overlaps; and a routing table you can now read as a list of address ranges. If your hand-computed answers match the calculator on all three, you can subnet — the rest is practice speed.

cheatsheet: Each bit taken from the host part doubles the subnets and halves their size
Block size is the number to carry: /25=128, /26=64, /27=32, /28=16, /30=4
Subnets always start at multiples of the block size
To find an address's subnet: divide the octet by the block size, drop the remainder, multiply back
First address in a block is the network, last is the broadcast, the rest are hosts
Unequal allocation: largest block first, each aligned to its own size
/30 gives 2 usable addresses — the standard size for a link between two routers
Blocks that fit: 2 raised to the difference in prefix length

checkpoint.prompt: Which subnet does 192.0.2.130 belong to, if the network is split into /26 blocks?
checkpoint.explanation: Block size 64, and 130 divided by 64 is 2 with a remainder, so 2 x 64 = 128. Verified against a calculator along with the other three cases in the lesson.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the network address of 172.16.5.0/20?
checkpoint.explanation: A /20 has a block size of 16 in the third octet, so networks start at 172.16.0.0, 172.16.16.0, and so on. 5 falls inside the first block. Verified: broadcast 172.16.15.255, 4096 addresses.

checkpoint.prompt: Why allocate the largest block first when subnetting for groups of different sizes?

choices.B: Each block must start at a multiple of its own size, and allocating small blocks first leaves gaps that a later large block cannot use
choices.D: Small blocks cannot be moved later

checkpoint.explanation: Alignment is the constraint. Place the /25 first and everything after it fits; place the /30 first and the /25 no longer has an aligned home.

checkpoint.prompt: A link between two routers needs how large a subnet?

choices.B: /30 — four addresses, two of them usable

checkpoint.explanation: Two usable addresses is exactly two router interfaces. It is the smallest subnet that can carry a link, and real networks contain a great many of them.
